did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jephthah is described both as a “mighty warrior” and as the son of Gilead by a woman who was called a “prostitute.” From the opening of the chapter, the contrast between his military ability and his family status is emphasized.

Did you know? After his brothers drove him away from his father’s house, Jephthah fled to the land of Tob. There, men described as “worthless” gathered around him—people without a clear place or status—and he became their leader.

Did you know? Jephthah did not agree to return to Gilead unconditionally. He asked that, if the LORD gave the Ammonites into his hands, he would become the people’s leader. Thus, his return was tied from the outset to a permanent leadership position.

Did you know? After the people appointed Jephthah as their leader and commander, he spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah. This presents his appointment not merely as a political agreement, but also as a public event before God.

Did you know? The king of the Ammonites claimed that Israel had taken his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Jephthah’s response was that the territory had been conquered from Sihon, king of the Amorites, rather than taken directly from the Ammonites.

Did you know? According to Jephthah’s speech, Israel asked Sihon to let them pass peacefully through his land, but Sihon gathered his army and began a battle at Jahaz. Afterward, the LORD gave Sihon and his people into Israel’s hands.

Did you know? Jephthah claimed that the Israelites had lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and the towns near the Arnon for three hundred years, and he asked the king of Ammon why he had not raised his claim before then.

Did you know? Before Jephthah went to war, the text says that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him. Only after this does it recount the vow he made, in which he promised to dedicate to the LORD whoever or whatever first came out of his house to meet him.

Did you know? Jephthah’s victory is described with a count and geographic boundaries: he struck down the Ammonites in twenty towns, from Aroer to the area of Abel-keramim, until the Ammonites were subdued before Israel.

Did you know? Jephthah’s only daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. The text emphasizes that he had no other son or daughter, making her appearance decisive in relation to his vow.

Did you know? Jephthah’s daughter asked for two months to mourn her virginity in the mountains with her companions. When she returned, the text says that Jephthah fulfilled his vow to her and notes that she had not known a man; the chapter itself does not explicitly state how the vow was carried out.

Did you know? Following the fate of Jephthah’s daughter, an annual custom was established: the daughters of Israel would go for four days each year to commemorate her—to tell her story and mourn for her—the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.
